text: Section 2.1, paragraph 1, 'Hartzmark and Sussman (2019) show that the publication of Morningstar sustainability ratings for mutual funds redirected fund flows; their ratings concern funds, so any effect on the stocks those funds hold is indirect.'

evidence_anchor: text: Section 2.4, H1, 'The recognition channel predicts an increase. The preference channel predicts an increase for firms with high scores and a decrease for firms with low scores. The selection view predicts relative growth before coverage and no effect after it if the growth was permanent, or a decline after it if the growth was transitory.'
text: Section 2.4, H3, 'This is the test that separates the preference channel from recognition, because only the preference channel depends on what the score says.'

items.change_summary: Channel predictions were restated with signs (including permanent versus transitory selection, carried into Section 6.1), and an exploratory size-, country-, and cohort-purged score split was added next to the median split; numbers match r4_h3_residual_score.csv and r4_h3_score_size.csv.

residual_gap.text: H3 is not presented in the abstract or Introduction as the preference-channel test with its estimate, its non-significance, and its minimum detectable effect: the abstract says only 'whatever the level of the score' and the Introduction says the effect 'does not differ' between high- and low-score firms, which reads a non-significant test (MDE 0.111 to 0.113) as equality. State the H3 estimate, p-value, and MDE where H3 is summarized and replace 'does not differ' / 'whatever the level of the score' with non-detection language.

new_issues.description: The Malaysian 2021-2022 wave is characterized as 'a wholesale expansion' (abstract Findings), 'a wave that extended coverage across a whole market' (Section 1), 'the wholesale Malaysian expansion' (Section 6.1), and 'coverage extended across a whole market' (Section 6.3), and the abstract concludes that 'exchange-wide coverage avoids that tilt'. The manuscript's own counts contradict this: the wave covered 289 firms while 565 Malaysian non-financial firms were never scored (Section 5.1; r4_malaysia_never_scored.csv), and a further 83 Malaysian firms were first scored in 2023 (Table S2). The data do not record the provider's coverage rule (Section 3.1), so 'wholesale' versus 'selective' is an interpretation, not an observation. The selective-versus-wholesale contrast is the revision's main new framing, so the overstatement reaches the abstract, Introduction, Discussion, and implications.

The exchange implication's lack of design bounds is graded under RR2-15; this record concerns the factual claim across all locations.

new_issues.description: The 'selective waves' claim is not supported for the 'all other cohorts' group. Section 5.3 says these 278 firms 'entered coverage a few at a time' and 'show the same pattern', and Section 6.1 says that in selective waves firms entered 'after their MTB ratio and market capitalization had grown faster'. But Table S2 shows the group includes 109 firms first scored in 2023 (83 Malaysian) and 31 and 26 Thai firms in 2021 and 2022, so they did not enter a few at a time; their market-capitalization pre-trend test gives p = 0.652 with an event-year −5 estimate of −0.077 (p = 0.26), so no market-capitalization run-up is detected; and their MTB e = −5 estimate (−0.103, 95% interval −0.213 to 0.004) is no larger than the e = −2 estimate (−0.108), so the pattern is a gap that closes in the base year rather than the same gradual run-up (r4_event_profiles.csv, r4_pretrend_tests.csv). The wave boundaries (Malaysia 2021-2022 only; Thailand and Singapore 2019-2020 only) were set after seeing Table S2.

new_issues.description: The abstract attributes the pooled MTB run-up to the selective waves: 'Firms that entered through selective coverage waves had outgrown comparable unscored firms beforehand: ... their market-to-book (MTB) ratio grew 10.0 percent more.' The 10.0 percent is the pooled estimate over all 675 firms, including the Malaysian wave the next sentence says had no run-up (r4_runup.csv); the selective-wave estimates are 33.1 percent (Thailand and Singapore) and 10.8 percent (other cohorts). Section 5.7 repeats the conflation ('the growth that precedes selective coverage' for the pooled run-up).
new_issues.location_anchor: text: Abstract, Findings, 'Firms that entered through selective coverage waves had outgrown comparable unscored firms beforehand: from five years before the first score to the year before it, their market-to-book (MTB) ratio grew 10.0 percent more.'
new_issues.competence_basis: Methodology seat; number traced to r4_runup.csv (pooled, est_e5 −0.0949) and r4_event_profiles.csv wave rows.
new_issues.attribution_evidence: v3 abstract attributed the 10.0 percent to 'scored firms' (all firms); the 'selective coverage waves' subject is added in v4 (diff_v3_to_v4.patch, abstract Findings).
new_issues.non_match_rationale: RR2-13 concerns intervals and the MTB joint test where run-up figures appear; it does not cover attributing the pooled figure to a subgroup.

new_issues.description: Section 3.1 argues that the Malaysian wave is unrelated to the November 2022 Bursa-LSEG agreement because it 'began in fiscal 2021, before the November 2022 agreement'. Section 3.2 states that the first scored fiscal year can precede publication by one year or more and that history may have been filled in when a firm entered coverage, so fiscal-2021 and fiscal-2022 first scores may have been produced after November 2022. The timing argument therefore does not follow from the data as described.
new_issues.location_anchor: text: Section 3.1, paragraph 3, 'The Malaysian wave began in fiscal 2021, before the November 2022 agreement, which concerned FTSE Russell scores.'
new_issues.competence_basis: Domain seat; internal consistency check between Section 3.1 and Section 3.2 (timing and backfilling).
new_issues.attribution_evidence: The sentence is added in v4 (diff_v3_to_v4.patch, Section 3.1 paragraph 3); v3 did not relate the wave to the agreement.
new_issues.non_match_rationale: RR2-7 asks that the relation to the November 2022 arrangement be addressed with what is publicly known; v4 addresses it, and this record concerns the internal contradiction of the argument used, not the absence of the discussion.

new_issues.description: The within-cohort re-based baseline estimates (−0.083 and −0.167 for event years 3 and 4) are reported without standard errors or intervals (r4_rebased_within_cohort.csv contains point estimates only), yet Sections 5.4 and 6.1 draw an inferential conclusion from them: 'Both specifications therefore show that early cohorts lost value relative to never-scored firms in their third and fourth years of coverage.'
new_issues.location_anchor: text: Section 5.4, paragraph 2, 'Re-based within each cohort to the first scored year, the baseline estimates for event years 3 and 4 are −0.083 and −0.167 ... Both specifications therefore show that early cohorts lost value'
new_issues.competence_basis: Methodology seat; checked project_R/outputs/r4_rebased_within_cohort.csv columns (no SE or CI).
new_issues.attribution_evidence: The re-basing analysis and the sentence are new in v4 (diff_v3_to_v4.patch, Section 5.4 paragraph 2).
new_issues.non_match_rationale: RR2-8 asks for the R10 profile, a g − 1 rerun, and which specification governs; it does not cover the inferential status of a new reconciliation estimate.

new_issues.description: The Introduction misdescribes the preference channel: 'Under ESG preferences, investors pay more for assets they can classify as sustainable and less for those they cannot (Pástor et al., 2021; Pedersen et al., 2021)'. The cited models price green versus brown assets, not classifiable versus unclassifiable assets; the next clause ('raise the value of firms revealed as green and lower the value of firms revealed as brown') states the cited prediction correctly, so the sentence is internally inconsistent.
new_issues.location_anchor: text: Section 1, paragraph 2, 'Under ESG preferences, investors pay more for assets they can classify as sustainable and less for those they cannot'
new_issues.competence_basis: Domain seat; knowledge of the cited equilibrium models (green/brown tastes).
new_issues.attribution_evidence: The sentence is new in v4 (Section 1 paragraph 2 rewritten in diff_v3_to_v4.patch); v3 stated that investors 'accept lower expected returns on assets they can classify as sustainable' without the unclassifiable contrast.
new_issues.non_match_rationale: RR2-3 asks for per-channel predictions in the hypotheses; this record concerns a misdescription of a cited source in the Introduction, not the hypotheses' structure.
